 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton, right, and Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump participate in a town hall debate at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri, on Oct. 9, 2016. (Rick Wilking/Reuters) 
 By Kaivan Shroff | Special to the Tribune PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Ten years ago this November, Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton lost to Republican Donald Trump. Eerily, almost everything she warned about him has since happened. She said he was Vladimir Putin’s puppet — he just recently defied bipartisan sanctions against the Russian dictator. She said he would refuse to accept an election he lost — then Jan. 6 happened. She said a man who could be baited with a tweet couldn’t be trusted with nuclear weapons and that Trump would shred the Iran deal and risk war. She said Roe v. Wade would be overturned. She even warned his tariffs would start a trade war with China and drive prices up for American consumers.
 None of it worked at the time, but it all checked out. Many of us who were on the campaign treat that record as vindication. Perhaps it should read as a warning of its own.
 Clinton’s accuracy in describing Trump was never the problem. But Democrats keep making one kind of argument — a verdict on Trump — when elections turn on the other kind — an explanation of why a voter’s own life got harder and what will fix it. Ten years in, despite being on track for big midterms wins, they still seem to be missing this lesson.
 Trump condemns his opponents constantly, but he also — always — does the thing Democrats most often don’t. He hands people a cause or a culprit — and a cure. Your plant closed because of NAFTA. Your wages stalled because of immigrants. Canada is the enemy! Almost none of it holds up substantively. Still, it works because the packaging is compelling: It tells a person why her life got harder and what to do about it.
 Stating the obvious — that Trump is “temperamentally unfit” — does nothing to persuade a voter looking for an explanation for their problems. It’s a conclusion about somebody else, and it asks a voter to care about the personality of a man she has most likely already made up her mind about.
 I worked on that campaign’s digital team. Every day we put out the clip, the quote, the documentary evidence, the contradictory video, on a theory nobody ever seemed to name — that exposure was the only thing standing between a reachable voter and our verdict on Trump. What we never took seriously was that millions of people already knew exactly who Trump was and had weighed him against something they wanted more.
 Ironically, Clinton herself had already diagnosed the issue. During the same September 2016 speech that produced the much-litigated “basket of deplorables” moment, Clinton actually completed the sentiment by describing a less-discussed second group of Trump supporters, “that other basket of people, who are people who feel that government has let them down, nobody cares about them, nobody worries about what happens to their lives and their futures, and they are just desperate for change. It doesn’t really even matter where it comes from. They don’t buy everything (Trump) says, but he seems to hold out some hope that their lives will be different. They won’t wake up and see their jobs disappear, lose a kid to heroin, feel like they’re in a dead end. Those are people we have to understand and empathize with as well.”
 But notice where she said it. She said it at a fundraiser with Barbra Streisand to a room full of donors. Her solution was to offer kindness and compassion — not to name an enemy and a fix. Trump spent 2016 telling those same people who had caused their pain and what he was going to do to make it better. The former is a nice sentiment. The latter is an argument, as detached from the facts as it may be. The first basket was the verdict — and that is the one voters most heard about during the campaign cycle.
 To be clear, this isn’t a rehashing about one candidate’s weaknesses. I continue to believe Clinton was one of the most formidable and qualified contenders for president in the nation’s history. But she ran the play the party believed in and still seems to.
 You can see the shared instinct in the numbers. In the final 10 days of 2016, roughly 9 in 10 Clinton ads were about Trump’s personal failings. This midterms cycle, Democrats have spent more than $163 million on ads mentioning Trump almost 180,000 times just since Sept. 1 .
 Democrats look likely to win big, while running that same argument harder than ever. Here’s what shifted — Clinton’s warnings have become receipts. Voters now have the consequences of his presidency to blame.
 Joe Biden, too, ran the purest version anyone has run of the “focus on Trump” strategy — a campaign about the “battle for the soul of the nation.” But look at the context of that moment: A pandemic overseen by Trump had killed more than 200,000 Americans by Election Day 2020 , the economy had cratered and the cost of Trump’s character and unfitness had become real. Voters didn’t need Biden to warn them of what Trump would do — he had done it. That made it easy to point to him as the cause or culprit. The catastrophe did the work. 
 Four years later, Democrats stuck to the focus on Trump, but he was no longer in office and could no longer be pointed at as the cause of Americans’ woes. Kamala Harris again warned us. She called out Trump’s Project 2025 agenda . She warned of Trump turning U.S. troops on American citizens .  It didn’t land. He wasn’t in power and was not a credible explanation of the problems of the day.

 The warnings didn’t get better in 2020 or 2026. They just became reality — the clear cause of the problem. Democrats should be careful not to mistake Trump’s current unpopularity for proof that we’ve figured out how to beat him or the next version of him. If the party still needs voters to experience the harm of Republican policies before it can actually win them over, we have merely learned how to capitalize on disaster — not how to prevent it.
 Clinton was right about Trump, but our campaign couldn’t convince enough Americans before it was too late. The next Trump won’t come with a decade of evidence against him.
 If Democrats still can’t persuade voters until they’ve suffered the consequences, we haven’t learned enough.
 Kaivan Shroff is a politics and culture commentator, attorney and former digital organizer for Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign.
